package.title: Tirzepatide and the Pill: Does It Affect Birth Control? #shorts
package.description:
Tirzepatide's US label warns delayed gastric emptying may reduce how well oral birth control pills work. The delay is largest after the first dose and diminishes over time.
Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea are common side effects. NHS pill guidance says vomiting or lasting diarrhea can stop a pill from being fully absorbed, so tell your prescriber.
The label advises switching to a non-oral method, or adding a barrier method like condoms, for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase. Ask your prescriber which fits you.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you. Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.

Sources:

Mounjaro (tirzepatide) US Prescribing Information, Eli Lilly, 2026

factcheck.summary: The science holds up. Lilly's own medical-information page confirms the tirzepatide label wording quoted in s2 and s4: it "may reduce the efficacy of oral hormonal contraceptives due to delayed gastric emptying" and the delay "is largest after the first dose and diminishes over time." The same page confirms the label's advice to switch to a non-oral method or add a barrier method for 4 weeks after starting and for 4 weeks after each dose increase. The NHS sickness-or-diarrhoea page (reviewed 15 Feb 2024) backs s6: vomiting within 3 hours of a combined pill, or diarrhoea lasting more than 24 hours, can make the pill less effective. Both Lilly label PDFs load, but they're compressed, so I checked the wording through Lilly's medical-information page rather than reading the PDFs line by line. The script gives no instructions of its own, sends viewers to their prescriber, and carries the don't-switch line, "Not personal advice" and the prescriber line. It's about 140 words. There are five minor issues, each with an exact fix below: one about precision, one about the muted-viewer test, one source correction and one on-screen tweak.

issues.claim: It points to a non-oral method, or adding a barrier method, for a time after starting and after each dose increase.
issues.problem: 'It' is unclear: the subject is the label, but s4's narration doesn't make that obvious. 'For a time' is also vaguer than the label, which says 4 weeks after starting and 4 weeks after each dose increase. Giving the label's timeframe isn't dosing advice, and it's the exact fact viewers search for.
issues.fix: Narration: "The label advises switching to a non-oral method, or adding a barrier method like condoms, for four weeks after starting and for four weeks after each dose increase. Ask your prescriber which fits you." On-screen: "Label: non-oral or barrier, 4 weeks". Change list item 3 to "4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase".

issues.claim: Vomiting or severe diarrhea may also mean a pill isn't fully absorbed, so tell your prescriber.
issues.problem: The claim is accurate (NHS: vomiting within 3 hours of a combined pill, or diarrhoea lasting more than 24 hours). But the on-screen 'Sick?' is broader than the narration and doesn't name what to watch for. It also needs to stay clear that this point comes from NHS pill guidance, not the tirzepatide label.
issues.fix: On-screen: "Vomiting or diarrhea? Tell your prescriber". Optional narration tweak: "Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea are common side effects. NHS pill guidance says vomiting or lasting diarrhea can stop a pill from being fully absorbed, so tell your prescriber."

issues.problem: Muted-viewer test: the spoken line "Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own" never appears on screen.
issues.fix: On-screen: "Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own. Not personal advice."

issues.claim: On-screen text: 'Ask your doctor or prescriber'
issues.problem: The on-screen text should show the exact prescriber line, as the craft notes require.
issues.fix: On-screen: "Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you"

issues.problem: The vomiting and diarrhoea guidance is on the NHS sickness-or-diarrhoea subpage, not on the combined-pill page that's cited.
issues.fix: Replace the src3 URL with https://www.nhs.uk/contraception/methods-of-contraception/combined-pill/sickness-or-diarrhoea/ and change the title to "Combined pill: what to do if you're sick or have diarrhoea" (NHS, reviewed 2024).
